analysis.investment_thesis: INOX India is a genuine quality niche business — 38% ROCE, 56% gross margins, and near-zero debt in cryogenic equipment with secular tailwinds from green hydrogen, LNG, and aerospace. However, at 41x EV/EBITDA for a 12% revenue grower with free cash flow turning negative in FY25, Mr. Market is pricing in perfection I am not willing to pay for.
key_strengths: Exceptional capital returns: ROCE 38%, ROE 29%, and Debt/Equity of 0.10 — the business earns far more than it consumes in capital
Structural moat via specialization: 56% gross margins on industrial machinery is extraordinary, reflecting pricing power in cryogenic tech with high switching costs and long certification cycles
Multi-decade secular tailwinds: green hydrogen storage/transport, India's LNG infrastructure, and ISRO-era aerospace cryogenics create durable demand beyond commodity cycles
key_risks: Valuation is punishing: P/E 53x, EV/EBITDA 41x for a 12.3% revenue CAGR business — any growth disappointment triggers severe de-rating
Free cash flow has collapsed: FCF went from ₹132 Cr (FY23) to ₹32 Cr (FY24) to -₹3 Cr (FY25) while net profit is ₹226 Cr — FCF/NI is effectively 0%, a serious earnings quality breakdown
Capex surge with uncertain returns: capex tripled from ₹44 Cr (FY22) to ₹125 Cr (FY25), consuming all operating cash flow; return on this expansion is unproven
red_flags: FY25 net profit ₹226 Cr but FCF is -₹3 Cr — a 100%+ divergence between reported earnings and cash generation demands explanation

FY2019 net profit (₹193 Cr) exceeded EBITDA (₹153 Cr) — an arithmetically suspect figure suggesting one-time gains or accounting complexity in the base year, distorting long-term profit CAGR to a misleading 2.7%
Promoter at 75% maximum ceiling — any regulatory or liquidity-driven selling pressure has no buffer
analysis.detailed_analysis:
INOX India is the kind of specialized industrial business I genuinely admire: it has operated since 1976 in cryogenic equipment — a field requiring deep metallurgical and engineering expertise — serving sectors where failure has catastrophic consequences. That translates directly into 56% gross margins (extraordinary for any machinery company), 38% ROCE, and a near-debt-free balance sheet. The company has methodically retired debt from ₹145 Cr in FY20 to ₹9 Cr by FY23, which is a mark of honest, conservative management. The secular demand picture is also compelling — green hydrogen requires cryogenic storage at scale, India's LNG terminal build-out is accelerating, and ISRO's expanding launch cadence needs cryogenic propulsion systems. These are not cyclical tailwinds.

The fatal problem today is price. Paying 41x EV/EBITDA for a business growing revenue at 12% per year requires a compounding miracle that history rarely delivers. More troubling to me is the FY25 free cash flow situation: the company earned ₹226 Cr in net profit but generated -₹3 Cr in FCF. Capex has tripled in three years to ₹125 Cr and investing outflows hit ₹141 Cr — all legitimate expansion, but the returns on this capital are not yet visible in operating cash flows. When earnings and cash diverge this sharply, I want to understand why before committing capital. Invert: what kills this investment? Either the valuation compresses to 25x EV/EBITDA (a 40% haircut with no earnings change) or the new capex earns poor returns. Both scenarios are plausible at current prices. A fair entry would be closer to ₹800-900, implying 25-28x forward earnings for a quality compounder.
